title: Heat Pump Rebates in Cape Breton 2026: Sydney, Glace Bay
desc: Cape Breton heat pump rebates for 2026: $300 to $600 per ton, up to $10,000 for moderate-income oil-heated homes, or free through HomeWarming. For older detached homes in CBRM.
h1: Heat Pump Rebates in Cape Breton
lead: Cape Breton Regional Municipality has much older housing than Halifax, and most of it is detached houses owned by the people who live in them. That is exactly who the province's heat pump rebates are built for. Here is what a home in Sydney, Glace Bay, New Waterford or North Sydney can claim in 2026.
cards_heading: What heat pump rebates pay in Cape Breton
cards_intro: We re-read Efficiency Nova Scotia's program pages on October 3, 2026. These are provincial programs. We found no extra rebate from the municipality, so a Cape Breton home gets the same amounts as one in Halifax.

cards.title: Ductless mini-split
cards.note: Through the Home Energy Assessment. Model on Efficiency Nova Scotia's list, installed by a certified installer.

cards.title: Centrally ducted
cards.note: On newly added capacity. Geothermal gets $600 per ton. Replacement heat pumps are not eligible.

cards.title: Moderate Income Rebate
cards.note: For homes heated mainly by oil, propane or other non-electric fuel. Stacks with the assessment for up to $10,000.

cards.title: HomeWarming
cards.note: Lower-income homeowners can get upgrades at no charge, including insulation and sometimes a heat pump.

cards.title: Oil to Heat Pump Affordability
cards.note: Closed to new applicants on July 2, 2026.

after_cards:
An oil-heated Sydney house

A family of four with an after-tax income under $120,750 heats a 1960s house with oil. They add a 3-ton centrally ducted heat pump: 3 x $500 = $1,500 from the assessment. Because they heat with oil and are under the income limit, the Moderate Income Rebate can add up to $5,000 more, as long as they are approved before the work. If their income is under the HomeWarming limit ($57,075 for two to four people), they should apply there first, because upgrades can be free.
sections: Cape Breton's housing, by the numbers

Statistics Canada's 2021 Census counted 42,310 households in Cape Breton Regional Municipality. Two-thirds of them (68%) live in homes built before 1981, and about one in five (21%) in homes built before 1946. That is a much older housing stock than Halifax, where 45% of homes predate 1981. About 74% of Cape Breton households live in single-detached houses and 71% own their home. The census also found 9.3% of households living in homes that need major repairs, higher than Halifax's 6.4%.

Put together, that means most Cape Breton households own the home they would be upgrading, so they can apply for these rebates directly. It also means the house itself may need work first. Ask the energy advisor whether insulation should come before the heat pump.

Cape Breton's average January low is about -6°C, close to Halifax, but the coldest reading in the last ten years was -28.2°C. A cold-climate heat pump keeps working well below the January average, so it can carry most of the winter. On the coldest nights, many homes keep their oil furnace, wood stove or baseboards as backup. Wood stoves don't count as a primary heating source for the Moderate Income Rebate, so if wood is your main heat, ask Efficiency Nova Scotia how they will treat your home before you apply.

Nova Scotia Power serves Cape Breton at the same rate as the rest of the province: 19.128 cents per kWh plus a $20.08 monthly base charge. A heat pump gives two to three units of heat for each unit of power in mild weather, which beats baseboards on the same rate.
The rules that trip people up

You must book the initial Home Energy Assessment before work starts. It costs $199, waived for moderate-income households. Upgrades must be finished within 12 months, followed by a final assessment. Replacing an existing heat pump is not eligible, because the rebate pays for new capacity. The Moderate Income Rebate needs pre-approval, so apply and wait for approval before you book an installer. The home must be your primary residence for both income programs.
installers_intro: Ranked by Google reviews (minimum five). We don't take referral fees or paid placements. Confirm your installer is certified for Efficiency Nova Scotia rebates before you sign.
claim_heading: How to get a heat pump rebate in Cape Breton
claim_steps: Check your after-tax household income against the HomeWarming and Moderate Income Rebate limits.
Apply to HomeWarming or the Moderate Income Rebate first if you qualify. Wait for approval.
Book a Home Energy Assessment with an Efficiency Nova Scotia delivery partner.
Get quotes from certified installers for a listed model. Ask how many tons of new capacity they are adding.
Finish within 12 months and book the final assessment to get paid.
faq: How much is the heat pump rebate in Cape Breton?

$300 per ton for a ductless mini-split, $500 per ton ducted and $600 per ton geothermal, through Efficiency Nova Scotia. Moderate-income homes heated with oil or propane can add up to $5,000, for up to $10,000 in total.
Does CBRM have its own heat pump rebate?
We found no municipal heat pump rebate in Cape Breton Regional Municipality. Homes there use the same provincial Efficiency Nova Scotia programs as the rest of Nova Scotia.
Is the oil to heat pump grant still available in Cape Breton?
No. The Oil to Heat Pump Affordability Program closed to new applicants on July 2, 2026. Oil-heated homes can still use the per-ton rebates and the Moderate Income Rebate.
Can I heat with wood and get the Moderate Income Rebate?
Efficiency Nova Scotia says wood stoves are not considered a primary heating source for the Moderate Income Rebate. Ask them how your home will be classified before applying.
Is there free heat pump help in Cape Breton?
Lower-income homeowners can apply to HomeWarming, which arranges and pays for upgrades. The after-tax limit is $30,187 for one person and $57,075 for two to four people.
